concept.name: DDD Strategic Context Mapping

relationships.description: Connects DDD Strategic Context Mapping to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Explicitly defining bounded contexts, their ubiquitous language boundaries, and the upstream/downstream integration relationships between teams and services in a complex domain.
spark.keyTakeaway: A single enterprise-wide canonical data model breaks down across teams; explicit context maps protect each model's integrity with intentional translation boundaries.

concept.whyItMatters: As organizations scale past 3–4 teams, sharing one monolithic `Customer` or `Order` schema creates tight coupling: a billing change breaks shipping, and every deployment requires cross-team coordination. Context mapping surfaces both technical dependencies and organizational power dynamics—showing where to build an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) to insulate your domain from messy legacy APIs versus where to publish a stable Open Host Service.
whenToUse: Multiple engineering teams own distinct business capabilities (e.g., Checkout, Fulfillment, Billing) that use the same nouns (`Order`, `Account`) with different meanings.
Integrating a clean new core domain service with a brittle legacy monolith, ERP (SAP/NetSuite), or third-party payment gateway.
Decomposing a modular monolith into microservices where service boundaries and team ownership must align (Conway's Law).
whenNotToUse: A small 1–2 team CRUD application where a single shared relational schema and unified domain model are faster to maintain.
Purely technical infrastructure splitting (e.g., separating a stateless auth proxy from a static asset CDN) with no competing business semantics.
Early-stage prototypes where domain boundaries are still shifting weekly and premature service splits would freeze wrong assumptions.
keyPoints: A Bounded Context is a linguistic and model boundary: `Product` in Catalog means rich media and SKU attributes, while `Product` in Warehouse means weight, bin location, and stock count.

Context Map relationships come in 9 canonical patterns—including Customer-Supplier, Conformist, Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL), Open Host Service (OHS), Published Language, Shared Kernel, and Separate Ways.
An Anti-Corruption Layer translates external schemas (e.g., legacy SOAP/XML or Stripe webhooks) into your domain's own types at the edge so external churn never leaks into core business rules.
Open Host Service (OHS) + Published Language (e.g., versioned OpenAPI, Protobuf, or AsyncAPI schemas) lets an upstream team serve many downstream consumers without bespoke per-team endpoints.
Shared Kernel (a shared library or database schema) requires synchronized releases between teams and should be restricted to small, stable core primitives.

examples.title: Insulating Pricing from a legacy ERP via an Anti-Corruption Layer
examples.scenario: A retail platform's new dynamic Pricing service must read base costs and tax codes from a 15-year-old ERP that exposes cryptic 4-character status codes (`STAT_X9`) and mutable XML payloads.
examples.outcome: The Pricing team builds an ACL adapter that polls the ERP, maps cryptic codes into explicit `TaxJurisdiction` and `WholesaleCost` value objects, and isolates ERP schema changes to a single translator module.

examples.title: Orders publishing an Open Host Service for Fulfillment and Analytics
examples.scenario: Four downstream teams (Warehouse, Notifications, Fraud, Data Lake) keep requesting custom fields on the Orders REST API, slowing down checkout releases.
examples.outcome: Orders exposes a versioned Kafka `OrderPlaced` event (Published Language via Avro/Protobuf in Schema Registry) and a standard Open Host REST endpoint, decoupling upstream release cadence from downstream consumers.

tradeOffs.pro: ACL protects your core domain model from external schema drift and ugly legacy semantics.
tradeOffs.con: Adds translation boilerplate, extra mapping tests, and maintenance whenever the upstream contract evolves.

tradeOffs.pro: Shared Kernel avoids duplicating common validation or money/currency logic across two closely aligned teams.
tradeOffs.con: Couples CI/CD pipelines—a breaking change in the shared package blocks both teams until coordinated.

tradeOffs.pro: A documented schema (Protobuf/Avro/JSON Schema) scales cleanly to N consumers with automated compatibility checks.
tradeOffs.con: Requires governance (schema registry, deprecation SLAs) to prevent breaking downstream consumers.

failureModes.name: Big Ball of Mud Shared Database
failureModes.description: Multiple bounded contexts read and write the same database tables directly, bypassing domain invariants and making schema migrations impossible without multi-team freezes.
failureModes.mitigation: Give each bounded context its own schema/database and enforce cross-context communication strictly through OHS APIs or domain events.

failureModes.name: Leaky upstream model (unintended Conformist)
failureModes.description: A core domain service imports a third-party vendor's DTOs (e.g., Stripe or Salesforce structs) directly into its domain entities, making vendor replacement a full rewrite.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap third-party SDKs behind an explicit ACL interface that returns domain-native types.

failureModes.name: Entity-service microservice explosion
failureModes.description: Splitting every noun (`UserService`, `AddressService`, `OrderItemService`) into separate contexts creates distributed joins and chatty RPC chains.
failureModes.mitigation: Draw bounded contexts around cohesive business capabilities and ubiquitous language boundaries, not individual database tables.

failureModes.name: Unversioned Published Language
failureModes.description: Upstream teams rename fields or change enum semantics in Kafka events without schema registry checks, silently breaking downstream projections.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce `BACKWARD` or `FULL` compatibility in Confluent Schema Registry / Buf and maintain dual-versioned topics during migrations.

commonMistakes: Attempting to design a single canonical `Customer` object shared across Sales, Support, Shipping, and Billing.
Using `Shared Kernel` for fast-moving business entities instead of limiting it to stable primitives like `Money` or `CountryCode`.
Building an Anti-Corruption Layer for an upstream service you actually control and could instead collaborate on via Customer-Supplier.
Ignoring organizational team topology—drawing context boundaries that cut across a single team or force two competing teams to co-own one codebase.
Treating Context Mapping as a one-time architecture diagram rather than updating it when teams reorganize or new integrations land.

sections.content:
## The idea

Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Strategic Design recognizes that large software systems cannot maintain a single, unified object model. A `Customer` in Sales (lead score, pipeline stage) is fundamentally different from a `Customer` in Billing (tax ID, credit limit, payment method) or Shipping (delivery instructions, geo-coordinates). Forcing all three into one class creates a bloated, fragile model.

A **Bounded Context** defines the explicit perimeter within which a specific **Ubiquitous Language** and domain model apply. **Context Mapping** documents how multiple Bounded Contexts integrate—both technically (APIs, events, translators) and organizationally (upstream/downstream power).

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider an e-commerce platform with three Bounded Contexts: **Checkout** (Core), **Fulfillment** (Supporting), and a **Legacy ERP** (Generic/External):

1. **Checkout -> Fulfillment (Open Host Service + Published Language)**: When a cart is paid, Checkout emits an `OrderConfirmed.v2` Protobuf event to Kafka. Checkout does not know how warehouses pick or pack items; it publishes a stable, documented contract.
2. **Fulfillment consumes `OrderConfirmed.v2`**: Fulfillment's Kafka consumer maps the published event into its own `ShipmentRequest` aggregate, discarding payment metadata it doesn't need.
3. **Fulfillment -> Legacy ERP (Anti-Corruption Layer)**: To reserve physical stock in the 20-year-old ERP, Fulfillment calls an internal ACL adapter. The ACL translates `ShipmentRequest` into the ERP's fixed-width ASCII/SOAP format, handles retry/idempotency, and maps cryptic ERP error codes (`ERR-402`) back to `InsufficientWarehouseStock`.

sections.content:
## Organizational dynamics & Conway's Law

Context mapping is as much about team communication as code. **Customer-Supplier** works when two teams share a backlog priority—the downstream team can negotiate new fields with the upstream team. **Conformist** applies when the upstream team (e.g., an external API like Stripe or a central identity provider) will not bend for you, and your domain semantics match theirs closely enough that translation isn't worth the cost.

**Separate Ways** is an underrated choice: if two contexts share only a minor utility (like PDF invoice rendering), duplicating 100 lines of code is far cheaper than maintaining a cross-team dependency.

## Context mapping patterns compared

| Pattern | Coupling Level | When to Pick | Typical Implementation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)** | Low (isolated at edge) | Integrating legacy or messy external APIs | Adapter/Facade translating external DTOs to domain types |
| **Open Host Service + Published Language** | Low (contract-based) | Serving multiple downstream consumers | Versioned OpenAPI, gRPC Protobuf, or Kafka Avro schemas |
| **Customer-Supplier** | Medium (negotiated) | Internal teams with aligned roadmaps | Contract tests (Pact) + sprint backlog coordination |
| **Conformist** | High (upstream dictates) | Commodity upstream with acceptable model | Direct use of upstream SDK/types in supporting domain |
| **Shared Kernel** | Very High (shared code/DB) | Two tightly coupled teams on core primitives | Shared versioned library (`common-money`) |

## Failure modes

The classic failure mode is **semantic drift across contexts**: Sales changes `Account.status = 'ACTIVE'` to include trial users, silently causing Billing to invoice free-trial accounts because Billing queried Sales' database directly.

Another failure mode is **over-engineering ACLs everywhere**: wrapping a clean, internal Customer-Supplier gRPC service in three layers of redundant DTO-to-DTO mappers adds boilerplate without protecting any meaningful invariant. Reserve full ACLs for boundary crossings where the external model is volatile, legacy, or semantically incompatible.

## Modular monoliths before microservices

Bounded Contexts do not require separate microservices or network hops on day one. Tools like **Spring Modulith** (Java) or **ArchUnit** enforce package-level context boundaries inside a single deployable binary—blocking direct repository imports across contexts while allowing in-process domain events via an outbox. Once a context's scaling profile or team cadence diverges, extracting it to a standalone service is mechanical because the Published Language and ACL boundaries already exist.

## Practical checklist

- Map every cross-team integration explicitly as ACL, OHS/Published Language, Customer-Supplier, Conformist, or Shared Kernel.
- Prohibit cross-context database joins; each Bounded Context owns its tables and schema migrations.
- Enforce schema compatibility (`BACKWARD` / `FULL`) in a Schema Registry for all Published Language events.
- Place Anti-Corruption Layers at the infrastructure edge (ports & adapters), never inside core domain entities.
- Use ArchUnit or module boundaries in a modular monolith before paying the operational tax of distributed microservices.

commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Ddd Strategic Context Mapping

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Explicitly defining bounded contexts, their ubiquitous language boundaries, and the upstream/downstream integration relationships between teams and services in a complex domain.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Fulfillment Context applies the primary invariant and coordinates with ERP ACL Adapter.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, ERP ACL Adapter experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Give each bounded context its own schema/database and enforce cross-context communication strictly through OHS APIs or domain events.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: A single enterprise-wide canonical data model breaks down across teams; explicit context maps protect each model's integrity with intentional translation boundaries.
Avoid trap: Attempting to design a single canonical `Customer` object shared across Sales, Support, Shipping, and Billing.
Avoid trap: Using `Shared Kernel` for fast-moving business entities instead of limiting it to stable primitives like `Money` or `CountryCode`.
When to reach for it: Multiple engineering teams own distinct business capabilities (e.g., Checkout, Fulfillment, Billing) that use the same nouns (`Order`, `Account`) with different meanings.
When to reach for it: Integrating a clean new core domain service with a brittle legacy monolith, ERP (SAP/NetSuite), or third-party payment gateway.

putItTogether.title: Putting Ddd Strategic Context Mapping Together
putItTogether.summary: A single enterprise-wide canonical data model breaks down across teams; explicit context maps protect each model's integrity with intentional translation boundaries.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Ddd Strategic Context Mapping before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The Pricing team builds an ACL adapter that polls the ERP, maps cryptic codes into explicit `TaxJurisdiction` and `WholesaleCost` value objects, and isolates ERP schema changes to a single translator module.
